content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors provide a novel neural network certification scheme leveraging input-convex neural networks and a small Lipschitz featurization map. This provides a certificate that is similar to those provided by Lipschitz-bounds, but works in the special (and common) use case where we wish to certify asymmetrically. The results are impressive for L1-bounded adversaries, but fail to surpass slower randomized smoothing baselines in the L2/Linf adversarial threat models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The problem of asymmetric certified robustness is novel and well-motivated to be of significant importance.
- The featurization of the non-convex portion of the feature-convex neural networks is rather clever and appendix B provides a great motivating example 
- The proposed approach is vastly more efficient than competing randomized smoothing baselines.
- The theoretical claims in Corollary 1 and Theorem 4 are very interesting and provide nice intuition for the theoretical power of convex neural nets. 
- The experimental results are reasonably thorough, and this method provides an improvement in the SOTA for L1 adversarial threat models.

Weaknesses:
- The inability to naturally and elegantly adapt this approach to multiclass settings is a limitation.
- The L-infinity and L2 results tucked away in the appendix are not impressive. Unfortunately it seems that this approach is unable to overcome RS on L2/Linf domains (but can certify more quickly)
- The expressibility theorems in Prop1,2 and Theorem2,3 are not that surprising or interesting. 

Questions: 
- on the asymmetric case, how do other certification methods (such as AlphaBetaCrown) fare? It'd be great to see some more classical deterministic verification baselines included in the experimentation section
- similarly, how much of the shortcomings in the L2/Linf experimentation come from the feature-convex neural net being highly non-lipschitz? Have you experimented with stronger Lipschitz regularization techniques (such as adversarial training) or Lipschitz neural networks?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is well-written, outlines the relevant work adequately, and clearly delineates the novelties of this approach.

Novelty: The work is a fairly simple combination of Lipschitz feature maps and the input-convex neural networks of Amos et al. However, the application of convex neural nets to Lipschitz-based certification is novel and interesting. 

Reproducibility: Enough details were included in the paper that, alongside with the provided codebase, I feel confident I could reproduce the experimental results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall this work provides a novel take on the certification problem, and employs a simple but interesting hack to input-convex neural nets to yield expressible and certifiable neural nets. The power of these networks is demonstrated theoretically, in addition to some very interesting properties about convex separability of datasets in high dimensions. The certificates provided overcome the state-of-the-art in the L1 adversarial domain, but fall short in L2/Linfinity domains.

content.title: Response to Reviewer2ZAQ
content.comment:
"The inability to naturally and elegantly adapt this approach to multiclass settings is a limitation."

While this is indeed a valid limitation that offers room for future extensions, we emphasize that practical adversarial scenarios are often binary, as outlined in Section 1. We believe our contributions are valuable in this more focused setting.

"The L-infinity and L2 results tucked away in the appendix are not impressive."

We note that while our method does not strictly outperform all baselines across all norms, it has a number of significant advantages that make it more practically relevant: namely, determinism, fast runtime, and closed-form certified radii.

"The expressibility theorems in Prop1,2 and Theorem2,3 are not that surprising or interesting."

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer's characterization. Our theoretical results highlight a surprising gap between the theory and practice of ICNNs; namely, even though the typical ML paradigm of overfitting to the training dataset should be possible, it is not achieved in practice, indicating room for improvement in the training of ICNNs. This analysis is novel in the literature.

"On the asymmetric case, how do other certification methods..."

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this relevant comparison and will consider it in future iterations on the manuscript.

"Similarly, how much of the shortcomings in the L2/Linf experimentation come from the feature-convex neural net being highly non-lipschitz?"

We clarify that our certified regions are not derived from Lipschitzness of our convex network (besides the initial feature map): rather, they are derived from convex function tangent plane underapproximations. The Lipschitz constant within a certified region can in fact be arbitrarily large. Consider a hypothetical scalar input classification function $g(x) = x^2 + 1$ with an identity feature map; at $x=0$, this can be globally certified to produce positive ouptuts using a tangent plane underapproximation (namely, the horizontal line through $(0,1)$), while the Lipschitz constant is unbounded.

That being said, as our certified radii scale inversely with the gradient norm, controlling the classifier sensitivity to inputs is crucial. Incorporating regularization techniques such as adversarial training is something we are excited to look into going forward.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper considers a  task in the area of certified adversarial robustness. Concretely, asymmetric certification. Here the adversary is expected to be interested only in swinging decisions in one direction; e.g., spam -> ok 

The certification task is solved by using input-convex neural networks with prepended Lipschitz mapping for which a one-sided certified radius is provided.

Additionally, the paper shows several properties of convex neural networks justifying their usage.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper proposes a method how to certify class 1 against $\ell_p$ adversarial perturbations in a binary setting for input-convex networks. The method is application of a standard technique of convex analysis. The empirical performance is demonstrated on four tasks; MNIST 3 vs 8, CIFAR10 cat vs dog, Kaggle cat vs dog, Malimg where the proposed method outperforms baselines in $\ell_1$ setting and loses to them in $\ell_2$, $\ell_\infty$ cases. As I will discuss later, I am not convinced that the comparison is sufficient (as I discuss later). 

### Strengths
* The paper is clearly written
* The claims in the paper are correct 
* The considered problem is interesting and the paper proposes a new method to solve it.

### Weaknesses
* The technical novelty of the proposed method is to use a standard tool of convex analysis to lower bound an input-convex function.
* The proposed method is applicable only in a specific setting, yet I am not convinced that it outperforms the competitors crafted for generic settings.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
* The paper is generally written in a clear manner. I have only reservations about the paragraph **Certified adversarial robustness** in Section 1.2. It completely ignores the two following important lines of work; 1) Interval bound propagation [1] and 2) bounding Lipschitz constants of networks. Especially the latter is surprising, since they are used as baselines.
### Reproducibility 
* The results look reproducible, the description is sufficient.
### Novelty
* Derivation of class 1 certificates for the convex network, which follows directly from the fact that the subgradient is a global underestimator of the convex function, followed by the Hoelder inequality.
* Extension of the universal approximation of input convex networks from regression to classification. Since binary classification is effectively a thresholded regression, the reduction is straightforward; although the approximation error is quantified differently in the two cases.

The remaining claimed contributions can be found in the literature.

* The convex separability is equivalent to the property that $\text{conv}(X_2)\cap X_1 = \emptyset$. Convex hulls have already been studied in this exact context. See, e.g., [2,3]. In the former case, this is a more detailed theoretical study with additional references to computational geometry, while in the latter case, the observations are almost identical to those made here with the CIFAR10 dataset. 

### Quality (of empirical evaluation)
* For random smoothing approaches, the choice of $\sigma$ is the key hyperparameter. The paper claims that sigma was chosen according to those used in  smoothing papers. However, the original publications considered more difficuilt datasets. It would have been more convincing if - following the standards of random smoothing - the experiments had been performed with multiple levels of noise.
* From the description, it does not appear that much effort was put into creating strong baselines for single-class certification; for example, certificate regularization is used in Lipschitz networks [4]. Is it present here as well? Only for a single class? Similarly, methods based on random smoothing benefit from adversarial training, while it does not seem to be present here. Also, most of the hyperparameters were taken from the original work, where the problem being solved was quite different. On the other hand, the proposed method seems to be tuned on a selected (somehow arbitrarily) set of tasks.


### Minor
* For Thm 4, the proof states "here the final equality follows from the independence of the samp coordinates", which is not true. The coordinates are independent, but the inequalities (=propositions) are dependent. In fact, we should ask how many random arrangements of $1, 2, \dots, m+n$ will have $1, 2, \dots m$ at the first $m$ positions - that is $(m+n)Cm$, which gives a better bound. I also note that whenever $d > n$, then the convex hull has zero volume, which almost surely implies convex separability.



[1] Gowal et al. On the Effectiveness of Interval Bounded Propagation for Training Verifiably Robust Models\
[2] Balestriero et al. Learning in High Dimension Always Amounts to Extrapolation. \
[3] Yousefzadeh. Deep Learning Generalization and the Convex Hull of Training Sets \
[4] Singla et al. Improved deterministic l2 robustness on {CIFAR}-10 and {CIFAR}-100.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, the paper does two things; 1) it picks up an under-researched problem and 2) it introduces a new tool to solve it which performs comparably to the existing general methods. In conclusion, I am neither satisfied with the treatment of the original problem, nor I'm convinced that it is worth considering input-convex neural networks for the task.

Specially, the paper considers a task of asymmetric certification against adversarial attacks. While the task is well motivated, it would be interesting to properly formalize it, discuss potential tradeoffs (robustness/accuracy/TPR x TNR etc.) and tune the existing methods to perform well on the problem before introducing a probem-specific method.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Ngmj
content.comment:
"The technical novelty of the proposed method is to use a standard tool of convex analysis to lower bound an input-convex function."

The simplicity of our certification approach yields deterministic, closed-form, and easily interpretable certified radii for all norms---we therefore view the simple form of our certificates as a strength, rather than a weakness.

"The proposed method is applicable only in a specific setting..."

See below experimental discussion.

"I have only reservations about the paragraph..."

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this omission and will augment the discussion in future work.

"The convex separability is equivalent to the property..."

We thank the reviewer for pointing out these relevant sources that support our experimental convex separability analysis in Appendix D. We emphasize that this empirical test is a relatively minor portion of our overall theoretical contributions, which we feel are novel and highly relevant to the problem at hand. Namely, we show that

(a) Any convexly separable data can be perfectly classified by an ICNN; and conversely, binary ICNN decision regions are necessarily convex (Theorem 3 and Proposition 2)

(b) Image datasets classes are empirically convexly separable (e.g. CIFAR-10 cats vs. dogs)

(c) Therefore, ICNNs can perfectly classify CIFAR-10 cats-dogs (Corollary 1)

(d) Dimensionality facilitates convex separability (Theorem 4)

Here (a), (c), and (d) are completely original, and provide a concrete expectation of what should be achievable with ICNNs. We note furthermore that [3] does not yield (b); [3] examines convex reconstruction of test set images from training set images of any class, while we consider convex reconstruction of one training class from another training class. Thus our empirical experiments in (b) are still required to establish our results.

"For random smoothing approaches, the choice of sigma is a key hyperparameter."

We agree that more thorough hyperparameter sweeps for baseline methods are necessary and will include these in a future resubmission of the manuscript.

"From the description, it does not appear that much effort was put into creating strong baselines for single-class certification..."

Various randomized smoothing implementations have used a wide range of training methods [Yang et al. 2020a]. The most competitive method for our l_1 certified radii [Levine & Feizi 2021] used noise augmentation, which we standardized on and is by far the most common way of training randomized smoothing base classifiers. We note that [Yang et al. 2020a] discarded adversarial training as suboptimal to alternatives. However, since we consider somewhat new datasets we will try all options in future iterations of our experiments.

"For Thm 4, the proof states..."

We appreciate the reviewer's thorough checking of our proofs. While we feel that the aforementioned line in the proof is correct, the reviewer's concern and proposed tightening both helpfully address a separate part of the proof.

First consider the step immediately preceding "where the final inequality..." Denote the event $x_k^{(i)} \geq y_k^{(j)}$ by $Z_k^{(i,j)}$. Note that this is a triple-indexed event. As the author points out, the events $Z_k^{(i,j)}$ and $Z_k^{(i',j')}$ are not necessarily independent if $i=i'$ or $j=j'$ (when considering a specific coordinate, i.e. the subscript $k$ is the same). But it is evident that $Z_k^{(i,j)}$ and $Z_{k'}^{(i',j')}$ are independent as long as $k \neq k'$, for any $i,j,i',j'$, since we are dealing with separate coordinates. Now note that the line in question factors over $k$ for clauses of the form: "for a particular $k$, does $Z_k^{(i,j)}$ hold true for some ${(i,j)}$?" Since each clause depends only on terms $Z_k^{(i,j)}$ for a particular $k$, the clauses are independent and we can factor over $k$ with equality. This is not quite rigorous as in general independence is not preserved by union, but for the specific random variables here it intuitively holds; we will make this more formal in a future iteration of the proof.

Where the reviewer's point is pertinent is the later step where we factor the probability of $x_k^{(i)} < y_k^{(j)}$ for all pairs $(i,j)$ into the product over $(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,M\} \times \{1,\dots,N\}$. Note here that we are factoring over terms containing the same $k$, so our inequalities could potentially be dependent, and hence the factorization does not follow from independence. We note however that the result still holds by simply changing the equality to a $\geq$. This follows by lower bounding the desired probability by the probability that all $x_k^{(i)}$ are less than $1/2$ and all $y_k^{(j)}$ are greater than $1/2$. The reviewer's proposed bounds tightening is something that we will explore incorporating into this step of the proof.

Finally, we note that $d>n$ is not generally satisfied, necessitating this bound (i.e. for CIFAR-10 $d=3072$ and $n=5000$).

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The proposed architecture is quite new and interesting, potentially leading to a new direction for NN certification. 
- The authors provide a very solid theoretical analysis for the proposed FCNN, laying a good foundation for future research works.
- The certified robustness properties are quite general in terms of different lp norms.
- The proposed method is very fast compared to randomized smoothing.

### Weakness
- Only asymmetric binary classification certification is considered, overall limiting the practical usefulness. Differences and limitations compared to traditional certification should be more clearly discussed. A related question: Could the investigated asymmetric binary classification certification be extended to common robustness definitions? Some existing approaches like [A] which generalize binary classifiers to multi-class with certification seem to be a good fit. A discussion in the paper would be quite helpful for future work.
- To make the experimental results more convincing, the proposed method could be evaluated on certain benchmarks in VNN-COMP21&22. There are some practical datasets and properties that fit the definition of asymmetric binary classifications.
- Recently SOTA deterministic certification methods have achieved great improvements in scaling to larger models, speeding up certifications, and generalizing to different robustness properties and architectures. Representative works include the recent VNN-COMP winner alpha-beta-crown, as well as other participants OVAL, VeriNet, Marabou, ERAN, etc (see VNN-COMP21 report for details [B] and latest VNN-COMP22 updates). As a certification paper, the paper neither compares with any of them in evaluation nor discusses them in related work...

[A] "Adaptive Verifiable Training Using Pairwise Class Similarity", AAAI’21
[B] "The Second International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2021): Summary and Results", arXiv'21.

content.title: Resonse to Reviewer R47y
content.comment:
"Only asymmetric binary classification certification is considered, overall limiting the practical usefulness."

We believe asymmetric binary robustness is a natural setting for a range of practical adversarial problems, as we discuss in Section 1. This relates to the idea that adversaries often attack an ML classifier with a specific goal in mind (e.g., don't be classified as spam) rather than just trying to induce as many mistakes as possible. We hope this additional structure enables the development of original, tailored certification schemes. The reviewer's interest in relating traditional certification to asymmetric certification is well-received and should be an exciting area of future work.

"To make the experimental results more convincing, the proposed method could be evaluated on certain benchmarks in VNN-COMP21&22."

We thank the reviewer for this helpful reference and will incorporate these datasets in future comparisons.

"Recently SOTA deterministic certification methods have achieved great improvements in scaling to larger models..."

We thank the reviewer for providing these additional comparisons and will incorporate them in future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of obtaining a classifier robust for a "sensitive" class against norm-based adversarial perturbations. The authors develop feature convex neural networks by combining input-convex neural networks with Lipschitz feature maps. This enables efficient computation of closed-form, deterministic certificates. Evaluation is performed on datasets for image and malware classification. The results show that the proposed architecture can achieve a larger robust radius against L1-norm-based perturbations than some of the existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The presentation of the technical ideas is easy to follow. This should make the methods presented here accessible to a broader audience.

2. The technical insights and theorems in section 3 are solid, novel, and interesting.


Weaknesses:
1. I found the evaluation results to be unconvincing and unclear (more on this below). 

2. The proposed architecture is tailored for the binary classification setting and handling norm-based perturbations. This limits its expressivity and generalization ability. It is not clear if the proposed method can ever be generalized beyond these settings (e.g., handling rotation perturbations).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: In Figure 2, is the radius for a single image or for the whole dataset? If the latter, how are the results for the different images combined? Comparison against randomized smoothing does not make sense as it provides guarantees on a non-deterministic smoothed classifier instead of the original deterministic one. In Fig. 2 (a), the authors do not provide details on how the L1-robustness radius of L_oo nets is computed. I also believe that this is a weak baseline as L_oo nets are not designed for L1 perturbations. The authors should consider comparing their method against other deterministic training methods such as (https://github.com/huanzhang12/CROWN-IBP) or (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.12715) that are better suited for L1, L2-perturbations. Further, the paper about L-oo nets is able to train networks for CIFAR10, so I did not get why the authors could not train it here. For L-oo perturbations on CIFAR10, the best results for the L_oo norm is from (https://openreview.net/forum?id=SJxSDxrKDr). The authors should consider comparing against it as well.

Quality: I am not sure how the empirical observations can lead to corollary 1 especially since no proofs are provided. This is not acceptable for a top-tier technical conference. Similarly, do you have a characterization of f for which Theorem 1 is valid? The statement "Thus, the certified radius given in Theorem 1 is always well-defined in practical settings." in Remark 1 is rather ambiguous. The authors do not provide any guidelines for how the Lipschitz maps should be designed. Can one replace the hand-crafted feature maps with a deep neural network with low Lipschitz constants such as in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.07559.pdf?

Originality: The architecture presented in section 2 is an extension of input convex neural networks. However, the theorems in Section 3 are novel and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the paper makes a solid contribution with new technical insights. However, because of the limitations of the current evaluation and the confusing statements mentioned above, I am marking it as below the acceptance threshold. I will be happy to raise my grades if the authors can address my concerns in the discussion period.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Uj8h
content.comment:
"In Figure 2, is the radius for a single image or for the whole dataset?"

The certified accuracy plot is to be read as follows: at a particular radius on the x axis, the y axis represents the proportion of the test set that can be certified at that radius. The y-intercept is therefore the fraction of the test set that can be verified at zero radius (the "clean" accuracy), and the certified accuracy proportion drops as the radius increases. This is a standard method in the literature for plotting certification strength.

"Comparison against randomized smoothing does not make sense as it provides guarantees on a non-deterministic smoothed classifier instead of the original deterministic one."

We agree that randomized smoothing certificates only hold with high probability for the smoothed classifier. This contrasts with our certificates, which are entirely deterministic.

"In Fig. 2 (a), the authors do not provide details on how the L1-robustness radius of L_oo nets is computed. I also believe that this is a weak baseline as L_oo nets are not designed for L1 perturbations."

Methods that only certify for a particular p-norm are converted to all other norms using the appropriate scaling factor, as described in Appendix F. Baseline methods considered generally only certify for just one norm, which can incur large scaling factors in high dimensions. In contrast, our method directly certifies against all p-norms without incurring scaling penalties.

"The authors should consider comparing their method against other deterministic training methods..."

Future iterations of our work will include more exhaustive baseline comparisons.

"Further, the paper about L-oo nets is able to train networks for CIFAR10."

The results reported in [Zhang et. al, 2021a] for CIFAR10 only yield ~60% clean accuracy for CIFAR10 across 10 classes. This likely is attributable to high accuracy for easily discriminated classes (e.g., ships generally have a blue background) while struggling with more challenging comparisons such as the cats vs. dogs setting we consider. As noted in Appendix E.1, we had success training their method for easy comparisons such as planes-versus-cars.

"I am not sure how the empirical observations can lead to corollary 1 especially since no proofs are provided."

The logic is as follows:
(a) Any convexly separable data can be perfectly classified by an ICNN (Theorem 3)
(b) CIFAR-10 cats vs. dogs is empirically convexly separable (Appendix D)
(c) Therefore, ICNNs can perfectly classify CIFAR-10 cats-dogs (Corollary 1)

"Similarly, do you have a characterization of f for which Theorem 1 is valid?"

Theorem 1 holds for any $f$ satisfying Definition 1, differentiable or not.

"The authors do not provide any guidelines for how the Lipschitz maps should be designed..."

More sophisticated choices of the feature map is an interesting area that we are currently exporing.
